name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.IcebergPersistenceConfiguration
comment:
Binds the ports to the Iceberg adapter. This is the only place in the deployable that knows a store implementation exists, which is what keeps {@code core} framework-free and the modules testable without a container.

The store is opened and its tables created at startup, on purpose: a catalog that cannot publish several tables in one action cannot honour INV-2, and the adapter refuses to proceed rather than falling back to ordered commits (ADR-009). Failing the boot is the honest version of that -- a lazily opened catalog would move the same refusal to the first customer.

Switched by {@code ltap.persistence}: {@code iceberg} (the default) here, {@code in-memory} in the tests, which supply {@code core}'s own harness instead.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.LtapCatalogProperties
comment:
How this deployable reaches the lakehouse. Deliberately a plain value type in the application root package: it is the composition root's own vocabulary, and no module has to know the catalog exists.

The property names on the left are this project's; the Iceberg constants on the right are the adapter's contract. Translating between them in one method means a rename in either direction is a compile error rather than a silently ignored setting.

methods.name: toIcebergProperties
methods.comment: The client-side catalog configuration, in Iceberg's own key vocabulary. {@code file-io-impl} is what makes this object storage: every metadata and Parquet file is written over the S3 API and no filesystem is involved.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.LtapCatalogProperties$S3
comment: The S3 settings this PoC actually uses -- MinIO, addressed by path, with static credentials.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.LtapServiceApplication
comment:
The deployable: one process in which the onboarding use case meets its implementations.

The package layout is the architecture (ADR-008). The classes in this package are the application itself -- the composition root that knows which store backs the ports -- and every direct sub-package is one Spring Modulith module: {@code party}, {@code relationship}, {@code contactpoint} and {@code onboarding}. Dependencies run one way (onboarding uses the three concerns, nothing uses it), and {@code ServiceModuleStructureTest} fails the build if that stops being true.

Nothing here reaches into {@code core}: the domain rules are called through the use case, so a transport concern (a status code, a header) can never become a domain rule.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.MalformedSubmissionException
comment:
A submission that cannot be read into the domain's vocabulary at all: a missing required field, or a value outside a vocabulary the domain names. Distinct from a domain refusal on purpose -- reporting {@code 422} for a typo in {@code relationship.type} would blame the customer's business case for a client bug.

It is raised while mapping, before any key is reserved or any transaction opened, so a malformed request leaves no trace and does not consume an idempotency key.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.Wire
comment:
Reading the request's text into the domain's vocabulary, with a code this project chooses rather than a message Jackson happens to produce.

The payload records hold {@code String}s for exactly this reason: the wire is text, and the moment it becomes a typed value is the moment a malformed submission has to be refused. Letting Jackson bind the enum instead would work and would be shorter, but the refusal would arrive as a framework message with no stable {@code code} for a client to branch on -- and the whole point of the edge is that every refusal is explicit (FR-003-004).

The first broken field is reported, not all of them: the domain itself refuses a submission on the first rule it breaks ({@code OnboardingService} returns one {@code Rejected}), so collecting a list here would promise more than the layer below can deliver.

methods.name: text
methods.comment: A required non-blank value. Missing text is a malformed submission, not a domain refusal.

methods.name: vocabulary
methods.comment: A required member of an enumerated vocabulary. Matching is case-insensitive and trimmed, so a client sending {@code "individual"} is not refused for cosmetics; the failure message names the vocabulary, because that is what the client needs to fix.

methods.name: date
methods.comment: A required ISO date ({@code yyyy-MM-dd}), which is how the lakehouse stores it anyway.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.contactpoint.ContactPointPayload
comment:
One contact point of a submission, as it arrives. It maps to {@link NewContactPoint} -- a contact point that is identified but not yet bound to a party -- because a request cannot be trusted to name the party each contact belongs to; the use case binds them inside the transaction.

{@code primary} is not validated here. INV-1 (at least one primary contact point) belongs to the domain, and duplicating it at the edge would mean two answers to the same question; the edge simply lets the domain refuse, and translates the refusal.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.ApiError
comment: Every refusal this edge can produce, in one shape: a stable {@code code} for the client to branch on and a human-readable {@code detail}. The codes come from where the decision was taken -- core's {@code OnboardingResult} constants for domain refusals, the exception types for protocol ones -- so there is never a second vocabulary to keep in step.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.IdempotencyKey
comment:
The client's promise that a submission is one intent, however many times it is transmitted (FR-003-004). It is a value type rather than a {@code String} so that "present but unusable" cannot be checked in one place and forgotten in another.

Any non-blank string is accepted, up to {@value #MAX_LENGTH} characters. The dojo's reactive idempotency sample ({@code 05_IdempotencyKey}) insists on a UUID; this edge deliberately does not, because a UUID requirement is a convention with nothing behind it -- what matters is that the client sends the same value on a retry, not what shape the value has.

methods.name: of
methods.comment: The absent header is the interesting case, so it gets its own exception rather than a {@code null}.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.IdempotencyKeyMissingException
comment:
Raised when a submission arrives without an {@code Idempotency-Key}. It is a client error, not a server one: the edge cannot make a submission idempotent on the client's behalf, because only the client knows which two requests are the same intent.

Deliberately not the same as a missing field inside the body: a submission without a party is a malformed payload, a submission without a key is a malformed protocol. Both are 400, but they carry different codes, and the difference is what a client needs in order to fix the right one.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.IdempotencyKeyReusedException
comment:
Raised when a key that is already known is presented with a different submission.

This is the one conflict the edge cannot resolve by itself, and the only reason a client gets a {@code 409} from the key itself: the first outcome is on record and belongs to another payload, so replaying it would answer a question the client did not ask, and executing the new payload would break the promise the key was given. RFC 9110's 409 is the right fit -- the request conflicts with the current state of the resource -- and the message names the key so the client can fix the bug rather than guess at it.

methods.name: key
methods.comment: The key, for logging at the edge. Never echoed wholesale in the response beyond the message.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.IdempotencyStore
comment:
Remembers the outcome of a submission against its idempotency key, so a retry is answered rather than executed (FR-003-004).

The contract has three parts, and each one is a decision rather than a mechanism:

  1. A key runs the work at most once. Concurrent submissions with the same key are single-flighted, so "creates one party" holds under a double-click as well as under a retry.
  2. A completed outcome is replayed, a different payload is refused. Same key and same submission returns the recorded status and body; same key and a different submission raises {@link IdempotencyKeyReusedException}, because replaying it would answer a different question.
  3. An attempt that throws is not remembered. The key is released and the exception propagates. This is what makes a retry possible at all after a commit refused by a concurrent writer ({@code ConcurrentCommitException}): recording that outcome would pin the client to a 409 for a key that never committed anything. Deterministic refusals are the opposite case -- the use case returns them, so they are recorded and replayed.

The key is scoped to the operation as well as to its value, matching the storage in the dojo's {@code 05_IdempotencyKey} (key plus {@code METHOD:PATH}). One endpoint means it does not matter yet; a second write endpoint would make it matter immediately.

methods.name: executeOnce
methods.comment: Runs {@code submission} at most once per {@code (operation, key)} and returns what to send back.

methods.name: find
methods.comment: The read side: what is known about a key, if anything.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.IdempotencyStore$Record
comment: What the store remembers about one key, exposed for diagnostics and for the tests.

methods.name: completed
methods.comment: Whether an outcome has been recorded. Until it has, {@code status} is {@code 0} and {@code body} is {@code null}: a key can be known and still be in flight.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.IdempotencyStore$RequestState
comment:
Where a key is in its life cycle. The vocabulary is {@code 05_IdempotencyKey}'s, deliberately: the same four states are what a durable store's {@code request_state} column would carry.

{@code WIP} is observable here only while another thread is inside {@link #executeOnce} with the same key (the lock makes it transient); it becomes a durable state the moment the store is, which is exactly why it is named now rather than added later.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.IdempotentResult
comment:
What one submission produced, in the only form the HTTP edge needs: a status and a body.

{@code replayed} is set by the store, never by the producer, and answers exactly one question: did this come from the record rather than from this call? It is what the {@code X-Idempotency-Status} header reports (ADR-009), so a client -- and the evidence table -- can tell a first submission from a retry without guessing from the status code. The status is replayed verbatim on purpose: a client that keys off {@code 201} would otherwise see a {@code 200} for the same key and conclude something different actually happened.

Everything the store is given is remembered. A submission that must not be remembered -- a commit refused by a concurrent writer, which the client's retry is supposed to overcome -- does not return a result at all: it throws, and {@link IdempotencyStore} releases the key.

methods.name: of
methods.comment: An outcome produced by this call, in the shape it will be replayed in.

methods.name: asReplay
methods.comment: The same outcome, this time served from the record.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.InMemoryIdempotencyStore
comment:
The single-process implementation: a map from {@code (operation, key)} to what was recorded, with one monitor per key. The monitor is what makes a double-click behave like a retry instead of like two submissions: the second caller waits, then replays the first caller's outcome.

What this does not do, stated rather than implied. It is not durable. The record dies with the process, so the guarantee is "a retry within this process's lifetime is answered", not "a retry is answered". The window is real, and the fix is already available: ADR-009's multi-table commit is exactly the mechanism that could publish a fifth table -- the idempotency record -- in the same transaction as the party, so that the key and the party become inseparable. Until then, a retry that crosses a restart is refused by INV-3 (a duplicate tax id) rather than replayed, which is why INV-3 is enforced in the store and not only here: the edge is a convenience, the invariant is the guarantee.

It also never evicts. A durable store would need a retention policy; here the retention is "as long as the process lives" and the memory cost is bounded by the number of distinct keys.

methods.name: scoped
methods.comment: Keys are scoped to the operation they were used on, so one endpoint cannot answer for another.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.InMemoryIdempotencyStore$Entry
comment: Mutable, and only ever touched while holding its own monitor.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.OnboardingApiExceptionHandler
comment:
Everything that ends a submission with an error, in one place, so that "which status does this produce?" has exactly one answer and that answer is tested ({@code FailureMappingTest}, {@code OnboardingSubmissionApiTest}).
What each refusal becomes
Raised byStatusCodeRemembered?
{@link IdempotencyKeyMissingException}400 {@code IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_MISSING}there is no key to remember
{@link MalformedSubmissionException}400 {@code MISSING_FIELD} / {@code UNKNOWN_VALUE} / {@code MALFORMED_FIELD} no: the key is not reserved until the request reads cleanly
{@link HttpMessageNotReadableException}400{@code UNREADABLE_BODY} no, as above
{@link IdempotencyKeyReusedException}409{@code IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED} the earlier record stands untouched
{@link ConcurrentCommitException}409{@code CONCURRENT_COMMIT} no -- see below

The last row is the interesting one. A commit refused because another writer moved the snapshot is the one failure the client should retry, so it deliberately escapes {@link IdempotencyStore#executeOnce} as an exception: the key is released, and the retry reaches the use case instead of being answered with a 409 that never committed anything.

There is no catch-all {@code Exception} handler. Adding one would swallow Spring's own protocol handling -- a PUT to this path would answer 500 instead of 405 -- and inventing a status for faults this layer cannot classify would be less honest than the framework's default 500.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.OnboardingRefusal
comment:
The one place a domain refusal becomes an HTTP status.

The split is not "which code looks worse" but whose fault it is:

  • 409 Conflict -- the submission is well formed and conflicts with state the lakehouse already holds (the party id, the tax id, the channel+value). The client can fix it by choosing different identities, and a retry with the same payload will keep conflicting, which is exactly why these can be recorded and replayed.
  • 422 Unprocessable Content -- the submission is well formed and internally inconsistent: a party with no contact point, or none marked primary (INV-1). No other submission or earlier state is involved; the payload itself has to change.

The {@code default} branch throws rather than defaulting to 500: core's {@code OnboardingResult} constants are the vocabulary, and if core grows a rejection the edge has not been taught, that is a build-and-deploy gap. Failing loudly at the first occurrence -- and in {@code FailureMappingTest}, which walks every constant -- is better than silently reporting a bug in the client as a server error.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.OnboardingSubmissionController
comment:
The HTTP edge: one endpoint, one required header, and no policy of its own.

Everything it could decide, it delegates -- registration of the request's shape to the payload records, the invariant to the use case, the status to {@link OnboardingRefusal} and {@link OnboardingApiExceptionHandler}. What is left is transport, which ADR-008 says belongs here and nowhere else: the header names, the replayed body and the status that carries it.

Two details are choices rather than defaults:

  • The status is replayed verbatim. A retry of a submission that returned {@code 201} returns {@code 201}, not {@code 200}: a client that branches on the status must not be able to conclude that a second party was created.
  • {@code X-Idempotency-Status} is set on every response, to {@code fresh} or {@code replay} (ADR-009 names the header and its {@code replay} value). Setting it only on a replay would make the first response and a retry differ by an absence, which is the harder thing to test.

No {@code Location} header is returned with the {@code 201}. The created identities are in the body, and a single-resource URL would have to be invented for a submission that creates four related rows; inventing one to be RESTful is not worth a header that would then need to be replayed too.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.OnboardingSubmissionRequest
comment:
The body of a submission: three nodes, each owned by the module that understands it. The edge does not restate what those nodes mean; it composes them into the one value {@code core} accepts.

Two asymmetries are deliberate:

  • A missing {@code party} or {@code relationship} is a 400: without either there is no request to speak of. A missing (or empty) {@code contactPoints} is left to the domain, which refuses it as {@code NO_CONTACT_POINT} (422) -- the edge does not keep a second copy of a rule the domain already owns.
  • The mapping happens before an idempotency key is reserved, so a malformed request cannot consume one.

Unknown JSON fields are ignored: the payload records are bound by name, and Spring Boot's Jackson default is not to fail on properties it does not know. That keeps a client free to send more than this version needs.

methods.name: toContactPoints
methods.comment: A missing list is an empty one: the domain, not the edge, is the authority on "no contacts".

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.OnboardingSubmissionResponse
comment:
What a successful submission returns: the identities of the three rows it created, in one unit of work (INV-2). It is serialized once and stored, so a replay returns the same bytes -- which is the whole reason the edge returns a body it has already rendered rather than an object it re-renders.

There is no {@code replayed} flag in the body. That fact belongs to the response, not to the submission, so it travels in {@code X-Idempotency-Status} where it can differ between the first submission and its retry without making the two bodies unequal.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.onboarding.OnboardingSubmissions
comment:
One submission, as the edge performs it: read it into the domain's vocabulary, claim the idempotency key, run the use case, translate the outcome. Four steps, in that order, because two of the orders are wrong:
  • Reading first means a malformed request is refused without reserving a key.
  • Running the use case inside {@link IdempotencyStore#executeOnce} means the claim and the writes are not separated by a window in which a second request could slip in.

The response body is rendered here, inside the claim, and stored as the text the client receives. Re-rendering it from an object on the way out of the replay path would give the same bytes today and a different status code tomorrow; storing the text makes "replay" indistinguishable from "first response" by construction, which is the property the tests assert.

methods.name: fingerprintOf
methods.comment: A digest of the mapped request, not of the bytes that arrived. The mapping has already trimmed the text, upper-cased the vocabulary and read a missing contact-point list as an empty one, so the digest is over the intent rather than over its spelling: a retry that differs in whitespace or letter case is the same submission, and a retry that differs in a value is a different one. Fingerprinting the raw body would get both of those backwards.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.party.PartyPayload
comment: The party node of a submission, as it arrives: text, because that is what JSON carries. The vocabulary is decided here, once, and a value outside it is refused with a stable code ({@link io.forest.lakehouse.service.MalformedSubmissionException}) rather than a Jackson message.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.relationship.RelationshipPayload
comment: The relationship node of a submission. It parses into {@code core}'s vocabulary but cannot build the row itself: a {@code PartyRelationship} needs the party id, which only the use case knows once it has decided the submission is admissible. That asymmetry is the point -- it is the reason the party node and the relationship node are separate concerns rather than one blob.

name: io.forest.lakehouse.service.relationship.RelationshipPayload$ParsedRelationship
comment: The edge's parts, already in the domain's vocabulary.
